column1: # The German review of ConstructIt's message bundle, as data (OP-29 slice 4).
# Slices 1 and 2 each ended with a person reading the whole German bundle — 85 corrections, then 366, in
# named classes. This file is what those classes became: `TranslationReviewTest` reads it and fails the
# build on the same mistakes, on every run, so a re-translation cannot quietly undo a decision made here.
# Three record kinds, tab-separated, `#` to end of line is a comment:
#   register <word>                                  an informal address the chrome does not use
#   concept  <english>  <approved|forms>  <rejected|forms>   one word per concept, both halves
#   except   <key>      <english term>    <the argument for excusing it>
# An `approved` cell lists every surface form that counts as the term having arrived — German inflects and
# compounds, so a stem is usually the honest entry (`extrudier` covers *extrudiert* and *Extrudiertiefe*).
# A `rejected` cell lists renderings the review ruled out; it is empty where nothing competed. Matching is
# case-insensitive substring, and the English side is matched as a whole word against the *prose* of the
# source message, with ICU argument names and selector keywords cut away first.
# ---- register: the chrome addresses the reader as `Sie`, settled in slice 1 ----
# DeepL writes the imperative about half the time when the English is imperative ("Click a body…"), which
# is 96 of slice 2's corrections. These are the du-forms that appeared; a quoted example does not count.
# Order follows l10n/glossary/en-de.tsv, which is what DeepL is given; every line there has a line here,
# and `TranslationReviewTest.theGlossaryAndTheReviewTableSayTheSameThing` is what keeps that true.
# ---- the arguments for the five keys a term of art is excused in ----
# Each of these is an English word that is a term of art *as a noun* and an ordinary verb or adjective in
# the sentence that names it. The glossary pins the noun, which is right; pinning the verb is what slice 1
# found turns *Fillet edge* into *round off the fillet*, so these are excused one key at a time.

column4: its points sweep no area is *enclose*, not the sweep operation — German says "umschließen"
upright is the adjective here (side faces standing vertical), not the upright member the glossary pins
skin them with Loft (ruled) is the verb; German says "überziehen" and keeps *Haut* for the noun
as above — the verb, not the surface
corners mitre {need} mm off the run is the verb; the German states the amount taken away instead
